DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
## What the study argues

The study recommends a district-wide weekly food waste collection from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot in 4,000 households. Its case rests on four claims:
- participation was similar across houses and flats, so one uniform service will do;
- the district will produce about 3,290 tonnes a year;
- sending that to Brookfield saves £74 a tonne, giving a net cost of about £490,000;
- the provisional new-burdens allocation of £520,000 covers that net cost.

I checked every figure against the study's own tables. The table arithmetic is correct, but three central claims contradict the study's own data:
- participation was not similar across housing types;
- the 64% participation rate used in the projection doesn't appear in the pilot;
- Brookfield can take only about two-thirds of the projected tonnage.

Once these are corrected, the funding margin all but disappears.

## What is sound

- **The pilot is real local evidence, and a good design.** It measured participation weekly by housing type, which is exactly what exposes the problems below.
- **The pilot mix matches the district.** Flats are 800 of 4,000 households (20%), the same share as across the district. The pilot's overall participation rate can therefore be applied directly.
- **The table arithmetic is correct:**
  - participation rates: 66%, 21% and 57%;
  - vehicles: 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 years = £141,400;
  - crews: 12 × £34,000 = £408,000;
  - total cost: £733,400;
  - net cost: £733,400 − £243,000 ≈ £490,000.
- **Contamination under 2%** at the plant is a genuinely good result.

## 1. Participation in flats was a third of the rate in houses

- Houses: **66%**. Flats: **21%**.
- §2 says participation was "broadly similar across housing types," and the author's description says it "held up across houses and flats." Table 1 shows the opposite.
- The conclusion that one uniform service will work is therefore not supported.
- **What the data suggest instead:** flats need a different approach. An outdoor 23-litre caddy per household often doesn't suit flats; communal bins, collection points or a different container may work better. The study should either plan for this or explain why the low rate is acceptable.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce

- §3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." The pilot's overall rate was **57%**. Weighting by housing type gives the same answer: 0.8 × 66% + 0.2 × 21% ≈ 57%.
- **Corrected tonnage by housing type:**

| | Households | Participating | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses (80%) | 41,600 | 27,456 (66%) | 1.9 | ~2,713 |
| Flats (20%) | 10,400 | 2,184 (21%) | 1.4 | ~159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | 29,640 (57%) | | **~2,870** |

- That is about **13% lower** than the study's 3,290 tonnes.
- **Corrected disposal saving:** 2,870 t × £74 ≈ **£212,500**, not £243,000.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

- Brookfield offers **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until its planned expansion in 2029.
- Projected tonnage is about 2,870 t on corrected figures, or 3,290 t on the study's own. That leaves **about 1,070 to 1,490 tonnes a year** with nowhere local to go.
- The rest would have to go to the plant 46 miles away. The study doesn't state its gate fee or the extra haulage cost.
- The £74 saving per tonne is calculated only on Brookfield's fee, so the saving on the excess tonnage is overstated.
- "Treatment is local," in the author's description, holds for about 60–65% of the tonnage.
- **The 2029 expansion is described as "planned."** The study should say how firm it is, and what happens if it slips.

## 4. The funding margin is close to zero

| | Study | Corrected tonnage |
|---|---|---|
| Gross cost | £733,400 | £733,400 |
| Disposal saving | £243,000 | ~£212,500 |
| **Net cost** | **~£490,000** | **~£521,000** |
| Provisional allocation | £520,000 | £520,000 |
| **Margin** | +£30,000 | **≈ −£1,000** |

The corrected position is roughly break-even even *before* the extra cost of sending more than 1,000 tonnes to the distant plant. That cost would put the service into deficit.

**The allocation is also only provisional.** The study says the Government "has indicated" funding will be provided. "Fully funded," in both the recommendation and the author's description, should become "funded if the provisional allocation is confirmed, with a likely shortfall."

**Capital is not addressed.** The vehicles are costed as depreciation, but £990,000 has to be committed when they are ordered in December 2026. The study should say where that capital comes from: a separate capital grant, borrowing, or reserves.

## 5. Smaller points

- **Statutory deadline.** My understanding is that the Simpler Recycling requirement in England was for weekly household food waste collections from 31 March 2026, with transitional arrangements for some councils. A start in April 2027 is after that date, so the study should state Thornbury's position.
- **Basis for six vehicles.** The study doesn't show this. Round sizes from the pilot, households per vehicle per day, would support it.
- **Missing cost lines.** The study doesn't say whether the following are included:
  - supervision and management;
  - cover for crew absence;
  - depot space;
  - the dedicated phone line and web page;
  - haulage to the treatment plants.
- **Timetable slack.** Ordering vehicles in December for March delivery, then training crews in March and starting in April, leaves no slack. If the vehicles are late, there should be a contingency such as short-term hire. The author is right that the plan works back from the lead time; it just has no buffer.
- **Seasonality.** January to June may not represent full-year yields. Yields around Christmas and in summer can differ.
- **Survey.** The 81% satisfaction rating needs its sample size and response rate. Respondents are likely to over-represent households that took part.

## What I'd ask the author to fix before Cabinet

1. Correct the participation claim, and add a flats strategy or explain why one isn't needed.
2. Replace the 64% rate with 57%, or with the housing-type breakdown, and recalculate tonnage and savings.
3. Cost the tonnage Brookfield can't take: the distant plant's gate fee, the haulage, and the arrangement after 2029.
4. Restate the funding position honestly: roughly break-even before the overflow costs, and dependent on a provisional allocation.
5. Identify the capital source for the £990,000 vehicle order.
6. Address the statutory deadline and add a timetable contingency.

## Bottom line

The pilot is good evidence that a weekly food waste service works well in **houses**, with high participation and low contamination. But flats participated at a third of the rate, and the projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce. Brookfield can take only about 1,800 of the roughly 2,870 tonnes. Corrected, the service is at best break-even against a provisional allocation, before the cost of the overflow tonnage. Cabinet should see those figures before authorising the vehicle order.
